subject: physics

moments.title: Hertz notices a peculiar effect
moments.body:
Hertz is producing electromagnetic waves with a spark-gap transmitter to confirm Maxwell's prediction. He notices that ultraviolet light on the receiver electrodes makes sparks easier to produce.

He reports the effect in passing — 'I will not say it has no important consequences' — but moves on. He dies in 1894 at age 36 without pursuing it.
moments.takeaway: A small anomaly tucked into a paper. It becomes the seed of a revolution.

moments.title: Lenard's measurements
moments.body:
Lenard quantifies the photoelectric effect. Three results puzzle classical physics:
- The maximum kinetic energy of emitted electrons depends on the frequency of light, not its intensity.
- Below a threshold frequency, NO electrons are emitted regardless of how bright the light.
- Emission is essentially instantaneous (less than a nanosecond), even at very low intensity.

Classical wave theory predicts the opposite: intensity should set energy, and weak light should take a long time to build up enough energy to release an electron.
moments.takeaway: Light's particle-like behaviour starts to assert itself in measurements that wave theory cannot explain.

moments.title: Einstein's heuristic paper
moments.body:
Einstein, age 26, working as a patent clerk, publishes 'On a Heuristic Point of View Concerning the Production and Transformation of Light'. He proposes light energy is concentrated in discrete quanta of energy E = hf.

His equation: K_max = hf - phi (phi being the work function). Frequency below phi/h gives no emission. Above threshold, K_max scales linearly with f. The numbers are testable.

quote.text: In accordance with the assumption to be considered here, the energy of a light ray spreading out from a point source is not continuously distributed over an increasing space, but consists of a finite number of energy quanta...

moments.takeaway: Light is quantised. The 'heuristic' word is Einstein hedging — most physicists think the idea is unphysical.

moments.title: Millikan's reluctant confirmation
moments.body:
Millikan spends 10 years trying to disprove Einstein's equation. He carefully measures K_max vs f for various metal surfaces and gets a perfect linear relationship, with slope h/e — Planck's constant divided by the electron charge — matching theory to within 1 percent.

Millikan accepts the equation but doesn't accept light quanta as physical realities. 'In spite of the apparently complete success' of Einstein's equation, 'the physical theory of which it was designed to be the symbolic expression is found so untenable that Einstein himself, I believe, no longer holds to it.'
moments.takeaway: Even decisive confirmation does not necessarily mean acceptance of the underlying picture.

moments.title: Einstein's Nobel Prize
moments.body:
Einstein wins the Nobel Prize 'for his services to Theoretical Physics, and especially for his discovery of the law of the photoelectric effect.' The Nobel Committee specifically does NOT mention relativity, which is still considered controversial.

The photoelectric effect remained Einstein's only experimentally tested theory at the time the prize was awarded.
moments.takeaway: Einstein's most famous work (relativity) is not what got him the Nobel. The photoelectric paper was the safest choice.

now.title: Photons today
now.body:
Single photons are routinely produced and detected. Quantum cryptography uses single-photon polarisation states for unbreakable key distribution (in principle). Photomultiplier tubes count individual photons; superconducting nanowire detectors achieve near 100 percent efficiency.

Quantum electrodynamics describes how photons interact with charged matter to ridiculous precision (the magnetic moment of the electron is predicted and measured to 12 significant figures).
now.open_questions: Can we ever 'see' the wavefunction of a single photon directly? How can quantum optics scale up to fully quantum computing networks? Is the photon truly a fundamental particle, or might it have substructure at energies beyond our reach?

reflection: Einstein's 1905 photon paper was his own most cited paper for decades. He later called the quantisation of light 'the only really revolutionary thing I have done' — even more than relativity. Yet most contemporaries took years to accept the picture. Why do specific revolutionary ideas struggle for acceptance even from people willing to use the equations?
